title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators (combined with a logical OR decision rule), and a matched sample of N = 300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline implemented under a frozen protocol (preregistration cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The preregistered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one initial LLM candidate was generated per paired intent and the same candidate was replayed to both arms (baseline is therefore not an independent-generation condition). The run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300 (shared candidate). The confirmatory outcome is degenerate: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); validators never reported forbidden reachability and the repair step was never invoked. Paired risk-difference = 0.0, McNemar two-sided p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Observing 0/300 violations gives a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Because the repair path was not exercised, this study quantifies that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the safety predicate under the chosen contract; it does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We archive the preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, per-episode validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to guide follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises productivity gains but raises safety concerns: generated configurations can inadvertently alter reachability, violate access-control policies, or expand attack surface. Prior system and survey work therefore recommend execution oracles, constrained generation, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as operational safeguards [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898]. However, rigorous confirmatory evidence that a verifier-in-the-loop GVR architecture reduces security-increasing misconfigurations under adversarial intents is limited. We address this gap with a preregistered paired experiment asking: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? Our contributions are: (1) a machine-readable preregistration that fixes a paired N = 300 confirmatory design; (2) a deterministic Dockerized execution using two deterministic validators and an explicit shared_initial_candidate generation contract to conserve model calls; (3) complete execution and analysis artifacts showing a degenerate confirmatory result (n11 = 300) and a post-hoc descriptive upper bound on baseline violation rate; and (4) artifact-grounded operational recommendations for designing stress tests that exercise verifier repair paths.
sections.related_work: Three strands frame our work. First, GVR and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness for code and Infrastructure-as-Code tasks by using execution feedback to direct repair, but improvements depend on verifier power, task difficulty, and model quality (e.g., TerraFormer, verifier-feedback systems) [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898]. Second, surveys and NetOps system papers document LLM failure modes—hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch—and recommend integrating validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to mitigate operational risk [https://openalex.org/W4415071524]. Third, emulation and testbed work shows that execution-based validation is feasible for research-grade evaluation, while warning of external-validity gaps to production networks. Our study differs by using a preregistered paired design with an explicit operational safety predicate (forbidden reachability), deterministic validators, and machine-readable execution accounting to produce verifiable inference under a frozen contract.
sections.methodology: Study design and preregistration: We preregistered study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1 as a paired confirmatory experiment (N = 300 matched pairs; 150 benign seeds and 150 deterministic programmatic adversarial variants). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). The confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05); prespecified 95% bootstrap percentile CIs were to be computed (analysis used 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729; this choice appears in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Sampling, exclusions, and contamination handling follow the preregistration: exact duplicates and fuzzy duplicates (normalized edit distance < 0.15) were excluded prior to execution; similarity flags are recorded in the analysis/contamination_summary.csv. Adapter contract and generation semantics: to reduce model-call cost the preregistered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired intent one initial LLM candidate is generated and that single candidate is replayed to both baseline and guarded arms. This produces exactly one hosted-model generation per pair (model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs) and eliminates independent-generation variance between arms; as a result baseline is not an independent-generation condition and the probability of producing discordant violating outputs across the pair is reduced. The provider-call audit (execution/execution_manifest.json) records 'shared_initial_generation' = 300 under stage_counts. Intervention arms: baseline = the shared initial candidate replayed directly as the baseline output; guarded = the same initial candidate validated by deterministic validators and, if a forbidden-reachability violation is reported, allowed up to one repair LLM call according to the preregistered repair policy (max one repair per pair). Repair policy and invocation rule are archived in the execution manifest. Validators and scoring rule: two deterministic validators were used for scoring and combined with a logical OR decision rule: a pair is labeled 'violating' if any validator reports the forbidden-reachability predicate. Per-episode validator_trace records (execution/scoring/*.json) include validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5' and validator_version = '5.0' and record repair_applied flags. Environment and determinism: experiments ran in deterministic Docker compositions using FRRouting-style images and deterministic orchestration; seeds and deterministic sampling parameters are archived in the execution manifest and per-task manifests (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Implementation and model configuration: the declared LLM for the run was gpt-5-mini and model_calls_used = 300 under the shared contract (see execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json for configuration details). Reproducibility artifacts: preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and model-call logs are archived in the evidence bundle (execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/responses/, analysis/*). Analysis plan: confirmatory McNemar paired test (alpha=0.05), 95% bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Prespecified sensitivity analyses treat technical failures as violations; no technical failures occurred, as recorded in analysis/missingness_summary.csv. Clarifying the practical meaning of the shared_initial_candidate contract: it reduces compute at the cost of inferential power to detect repair efficacy arising from independent model sampling; we discuss operational trade-offs in Results and Discussion.
sections.results: Execution accounting and provider audit: planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions), completed = 600, failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 300 under shared_initial_candidate semantics (provider-call audit: 'shared_initial_generation' = 300). Wall-clock timestamps of the run are recorded in the execution manifest (started 2026-08-28T22:15:28Z; completed 2026-08-28T22:50:41Z). Primary confirmatory outcome: complete_pair_count = 300; baseline_success_count = 300; guarded_success_count = 300. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). Inferential summary: paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and generated figure artifact analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg). Repair activity and verifier behavior: repair is attempted only when a validator reports forbidden reachability; across the run validators never reported forbidden reachability in any initial candidate. Representative per-episode scoring traces (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json and others) show validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false. Verifier concordance: archived per-episode traces show no disagreements across the two validators (verifier_disagreement_rate = 0 in the analysis artifacts). Practical consequence for the planned hypothesis test: with n11 = 300 and n10 = n01 = 0 the McNemar test is uninformative about the efficacy of repair because no discordant pairs exist; therefore the confirmatory test cannot demonstrate a reduction in violations by repair when no violations were observed in baseline. Post-hoc descriptive bound: observing 0 violations in N = 300 independent episodes yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the underlying baseline violation probability of 1 - 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%). We report this numeric bound as a descriptive constraint on undetected baseline violations but emphasize it is not a substitute for experiments that exercise the repair path. Representative examples: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (and baseline/guarded variants) and scoring traces execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json illustrate typical normalized configurations and validator summaries confirming no forbidden reachability for the sampled intents.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and boundaries: the degenerate outcome indicates that, under the chosen contract (shared_initial_candidate), model (gpt-5-mini), validator set, task generator, and emulator, baseline generation already satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for all preregistered items; consequently inserting a verifier did not alter observed compliance. This result answers whether verifier insertion changes observed compliance under this specific contract and conditions (answer: no), but it does not evaluate whether verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations because the repair path was never exercised. Design factors that drove the result: (1) shared_initial_candidate reduces independent-generation variance and therefore reduces the chance of producing discordant violating outputs across the pair; (2) the adversarial-variant generator used here (one deterministic perturbation per benign seed) did not produce validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the selected model and validators; (3) repair budget (≤1 repair call) constrained iterative rescue opportunities. Operational implications and recommendations: to demonstrate verifier utility for preventing security-increasing misconfigurations, experiments should (a) use independent-condition generation (separate LLM draws per arm) or increase repair-call budgets to permit repair to be observed; (b) strengthen adversarial-intent generation to target verifier predicates; (c) evaluate multiple LLM families and stronger oracles; and (d) increase emulator heterogeneity and incorporate live-traffic or device-specific behaviors to improve external validity. On reproducibility and artifact grounding: all preregistration, provider-audit records, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis outputs are archived in the evidence bundle (execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/raw_results.jsonl, analysis/*). These artifacts record provider-call accounting, per-episode validator_trace fields (including repair_applied flags), and analysis logs (bootstrap parameters and seed). Threats to validity: internal validity is limited by shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope; construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and validators adequately capture operational security risk; external validity is limited by synthetic intents and Dockerized emulation; conclusion validity is constrained by the degenerate contingency. These threats are enumerated and supported by the archived manifests and contingency artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We carried out a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation using gpt-5-mini across 300 matched intents under a shared_initial_candidate contract. The confirmatory outcome was degenerate: both baseline and guarded conditions passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair step was not invoked and the study cannot determine whether GVR repairs would rescue genuine violations. The experiment highlights that generation semantics, adversarial potency, repair budget, verifier strength, and model diversity materially affect whether verifier-in-the-loop architectures can demonstrate benefits for NetOps security. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to inform stress-testing designs that intentionally exercise repair paths (independent draws, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl, and the transformation logs are available in the execution manifest for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
